title: Cell theory, scale, and emergence mastery check

items.prompt: An observer holds a specimen at 40 cm and has the standard angular resolution limit of 1 minute of arc, which is about 2.9 x 10^-4 radians. The cells in the specimen are 12 µm across. Work out the smallest separation the observer can resolve at that distance, give the factor by which a cell falls short of it, and state whether the observer could establish that the specimen is built from separate units. Then say what a conventional light microscope, with a lateral limit of about 0.25 µm, would add, giving the factor there as well. Show the arithmetic and carry the units through it.

answer.correct: At 40 cm the smallest resolvable separation is s = d x theta = 400 mm x 2.9 x 10^-4 = 0.116 mm, which is about 116 µm. A 12 µm cell is smaller than that by a factor of 116/12, which is about 10, so the observer cannot resolve one cell from the next and cannot establish that the specimen is built from separate units, however carefully they look. A conventional light microscope with a lateral limit of about 0.25 µm sits below the cell width by a factor of 12/0.25, which is about 48, so it separates neighbouring cells with a wide margin and settles the question that the unaided eye cannot even address.
answer.summary: About 116 µm at 40 cm, a cell roughly ten times smaller than that, so no; a light microscope has about forty-eight times the margin needed, so yes.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for the conversion, which requires the distance in a length unit and the angle in radians and yields about 116 µm; a response that reports 0.1 mm as a remembered constant rather than computing it at 40 cm does not earn this point, because the whole content of the relation is that the threshold moves with distance. Award one point for the factor of about ten and the correct verdict that the cell is below the threshold. Award one point for the light-microscope comparison with its factor of about forty-eight and the statement that the instrument therefore resolves the cells. On a retry, run the same three steps for an observer at 20 cm looking at 18 µm cells, which gives a threshold near 58 µm and a factor near 3, and note that the verdict does not change even though both numbers do.
acceptableResponses: Any response that multiplies the distance by the angle with consistent units to obtain roughly 0.1 mm at 40 cm, gives a factor near ten against a 12 µm cell with the correct negative verdict, and gives a factor near fifty for the light microscope with the correct positive verdict. Values within about twenty per cent of these figures are correct, since the inputs are themselves approximate.
commonErrors: Quoting 100 µm from the lesson instead of computing the threshold at the stated 40 cm
Multiplying by the angle in degrees or arcminutes rather than radians
Reporting the threshold in millimetres and the cell in micrometres and then dividing without converting
Concluding that a light microscope cannot help because the cell is smaller than the eye's threshold
Giving the verdict with no factor, so nothing shows how far short the cell falls

items.prompt: A classmate writes: "Cell theory is only a theory, so the whole of histology rests on an assumption nobody has checked." Write a reply of a few sentences. State what cell theory asserts. For two of its propositions, name an observation that would have refuted it and say whether anyone was in a position to look. Then say what the word theory is reporting when a field uses it, and how that differs from the everyday sense your classmate is using.

answer.correct: Cell theory asserts that the tissues of plants and animals are composed of cells as their basic unit, that cells carry the attributes of life, and that every cell arises from the division of a pre-existing cell. Each part was refusable. The first would have fallen to a tissue found to be built from something other than cells, and two centuries of microscopy across plants, animals, and human organs were exactly the search for one. The third would have fallen to a cell shown to condense out of non-cellular material, which was a live rival account in the nineteenth century and was investigated and did not survive. The word theory reports that an explanatory account with stated assumptions and a declared domain has been put at risk of failure repeatedly across that domain and has not failed, so it is the strongest standing a field grants. The everyday sense, an untested private guess, is the opposite end of the scale, and using it to describe cell theory reverses the meaning. Histology does rest on cell theory, and that is a reason for confidence rather than a gap.
answer.summary: Three propositions, at least two with a stated refuting observation and evidence that people looked, plus the point that the scientific sense of theory reports survived risk while the everyday sense reports untested speculation.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for a statement of what cell theory asserts that includes both the composition claim and the claim that cells come from pre-existing cells. Award one point for two propositions each paired with a concrete observation that would have refuted it, together with some indication that the search actually happened; naming the propositions without a refuting observation does not earn this point, because the refusability is the whole argument. Award one point for the contrast between the two senses of theory, stated as survived risk against untested speculation, and for a reply that addresses the classmate's conclusion about histology rather than only correcting the vocabulary. On a retry, write the same reply about germ theory instead, keeping the structure: what it asserts, what would have refuted it, whether anyone looked, and what the word is reporting.
acceptableResponses: Any reply that states the assertions, supplies a refuting observation for two of them with evidence that the question was pursued, and distinguishes the scientific sense of theory from the everyday sense in terms of tested risk rather than in terms of certainty or of how many people believe it.
commonErrors: Answering that a theory is just a very well supported hypothesis, which leaves the difference as a matter of degree of belief
Asserting that cell theory has been proved, which claims more than any evidence supplies
Listing the propositions with no observation that could have refuted any of them
Correcting the vocabulary while leaving the classmate's claim about histology unanswered
Treating popularity or textbook status as the reason the account is trusted

items.prompt: Along a colonic crypt, signalling from the base falls off with height, so how much signal a cell receives carries information about how far up the crypt it has travelled. Which statement classifies that gradient correctly, and for the right reason?

options.text: Not emergent, because each cell has its own receptors and therefore carries the property itself.
Emergent, because a gradient is a difference across an arranged population, so a cell taken out of the crypt has no position left for a gradient to encode.
Emergent, because a crypt contains about 700 cells and a single cell contains one.
Not emergent, because every step in the crypt reduces to ordinary chemistry and physics.

answer.summary: Emergent, because position is a relation to other cells and a dissociated cell has none.
answer.reasoning: Both halves of the test point the same way. Look for the property in one cell and you find receptors and a response to a signal, which is a different property from a difference in signal across a population. Take the crypt apart while keeping every cell alive and the gradient goes even though every cell is intact. The receptor option makes the commonest error, which is to find some related property in a component and stop there. The option about 700 cells names number instead of arrangement; 700 cells shaken into a tube have no gradient at all. The chemistry option treats emergence as a claim that something non-physical has been added, which the lesson's definition explicitly denies: nothing beyond the components and their arrangement is involved, and the arrangement is doing the work. If you chose that one, reread the definition, because it agrees with your physics and disagrees with your conclusion. On a retry, classify two more: the mucus layer covering the epithelium, and a single cell's ability to manufacture a mucin protein.
commonErrors: Locating a related single-cell property and treating it as the property in question
Using the number of cells rather than their arrangement as the reason
Reading emergence as a claim that something non-physical has been added
Applying only the first half of the test and skipping the dissociation check

items.prompt: An invented research team drafts a protocol to watch colonic crypt renewal. Their imaging system delivers about 40 µm of resolution to the observer and can run continuously for six hours. The draft states three things they intend to report. First, the mean diameter of the crypt cells, to one decimal place. Second, the barrier property of the individual cells they observe. Third, that cell theory tells them every cell they see arose from a dividing cell, so that proposition is untestable and will not be examined. Judge each of the three, then say what the team would have to change to follow one cell from the base of a crypt to the surface, giving both the resolution and the observation time they would need and your reasoning for each. No real study, device, patient, or clinical procedure is described here, and nothing in this item is guidance for any real investigation.

answer.correct: At 40 µm the system resolves a crypt, which runs a few hundred micrometres, and cannot resolve a cell of 10 to 20 µm, so it can show where crypts are and how they are arranged and can show nothing about individual cells. The first report is therefore impossible twice over: the instrument cannot separate one cell from its neighbour at all, and a diameter to one decimal place claims a precision no method of this kind could produce even if it could see the cells. The second report is a category error. A barrier is a property of coverage across a joined population, so an individual cell has no barrier property to observe; apply the two-part test and you find a cell's own boundary, which is a different property, and you find the tissue barrier disappearing when the sheet is dissociated while every cell survives. The third report is half right and half wrong. Treating the proposition as established and not re-examining it is reasonable, because it has been at risk of refutation for well over a century and has not failed. Calling it untestable inverts the reason it is trusted: it is trusted precisely because a cell condensing from non-cellular material would have refuted it and was looked for. To follow one cell they would need resolution better than about 10 µm, meaning finer than one cell width, with more margin than that to see a cell's shape rather than merely register that something is there, and a light microscope's floor near 0.25 µm leaves ample room, so the obstacle is engineering rather than physics. They would also need days rather than hours, because the climb from base to surface takes about three to five days, so a six-hour run captures roughly a twentieth of the process.
answer.summary: One impossible measurement, one category error, one proposition rightly assumed and wrongly described as untestable, and a redesign needing sub-10 µm resolution and several days.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for the resolution analysis: the system resolves crypts and not cells, with the comparison made explicitly against both the crypt's few hundred micrometres and the cell's 10 to 20 µm. Award one point for rejecting the first report, and the point requires both objections, the resolution failure and the false precision; either alone is half the answer. Award one point for rejecting the second report using the two-part test rather than by asserting that barriers are tissue properties. Award one point for the split judgement on the third report together with the redesign; a response that rejects the third report outright has not discriminated, since assuming a well-established account is legitimate, and a response that accepts it outright has missed that untestable is the wrong word for something that survived being tested. The redesign must give both a resolution requirement below one cell width and an observation time of days, each with its reason. All four are required for full marks. On a retry, review a second invented protocol: an instrument delivering 8 µm of resolution that runs for a week but images only a single fixed plane through the tissue.
acceptableResponses: Any response that compares 40 µm against both the crypt scale and the cell scale with the correct verdicts, rejects the decimal-place measurement on both resolution and precision grounds, rejects the individual-cell barrier claim by applying the two-part test, separates the legitimate assumption in the third report from the incorrect word untestable, and specifies both a sub-10 µm resolution and a multi-day observation with reasons.
commonErrors: Rejecting all three reports without separating the instrument error from the category error from the vocabulary error
Rejecting the cell-diameter report only because the instrument is too coarse, leaving the false precision unremarked
Rejecting the individual-cell barrier claim by asserting the rule instead of applying the test
Agreeing that a well-established proposition is untestable
Giving a resolution requirement and forgetting that the observation must run for days
Naming physics as the obstacle to better resolution when a light microscope's limit is far below what is needed

rubrics.title: Computing a resolution threshold and comparing it with a cell

criteria.description: Award 1 point only when the threshold is computed from the stated 40 cm distance and the angle in radians, giving about 116 µm, with units carried through. A remembered 0.1 mm does not earn it.
Award 1 point only when the cell is compared with that threshold as a factor of about ten and the verdict is that an unaided observer cannot establish separate units.
Award 1 point only when the light microscope's 0.25 µm limit is compared with the 12 µm cell as a factor of about forty-eight and the correct positive verdict follows.

rubrics.title: Defending the standing of cell theory

criteria.description: Award 1 point only when the reply states what cell theory asserts, including both that tissues are composed of cells and that cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Award 1 point only when two propositions each carry a concrete observation that would have refuted them, together with an indication that the question was actually pursued.

Award 1 point only when the scientific sense of theory is distinguished from the everyday sense by surviving tested risk rather than by degree of belief, and the classmate's conclusion about histology is answered.

rubrics.title: Classifying a crypt property as emergent

criteria.description: Award 1 point only when the arranged-population option is selected.
Award 1 point only when the reason chosen is the loss of position on dissociation, rather than the number of cells, the presence of receptors, or a claim about physics.

rubrics.title: Integrated review of an unfamiliar observation protocol

criteria.description: Award 1 point only when 40 µm is compared explicitly against both the crypt scale and the cell scale, with the correct verdict for each.
Award 1 point only when the cell-diameter report is rejected on both grounds, the instrument's inability to separate cells and the precision the method cannot produce.
Award 1 point only when the individual-cell barrier claim is rejected by applying the two-part test rather than by asserting that barriers belong to tissues.

Award 1 point only when the third report is split into its legitimate assumption and its incorrect claim of untestability, and the redesign supplies both a resolution below one cell width and a multi-day observation, each with a reason.
